questions.question:
Let $\overrightarrow{OP}$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}$ be the position vectors of points $P$, $Q$, $R$ respectively. It is given that
$$\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\8\end{pmatrix},\qquad \overrightarrow{QR}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda+2\\2\\\mu-5\end{pmatrix}.$$
What are the values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ if $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are collinear?
questions.answer: $P,Q,R$ are collinear when $\overrightarrow{QR}=k\overrightarrow{PQ}$. The $y$-components give $2=k(1)$, so $k=2$ and $\overrightarrow{QR}=2\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\2\\16\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $\lambda+2=-8\Rightarrow\lambda=-10$ and $\mu-5=16\Rightarrow\mu=21$ (D).

questions.question:
Consider the two lines with vector equations
$$\mathbf{r}_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{and}\quad \mathbf{r}_2=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\2\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}3\\-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Which of the following is the exact value of the angle between the two lines?
questions.answer: Use the direction vectors $\mathbf{d}_1=(-1,2,1)$ and $\mathbf{d}_2=(3,-4,-2)$. $\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=-3-8-2=-13$, $|\mathbf{d}_1|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf{d}_2|=\sqrt{29}$, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-13}{\sqrt6\sqrt{29}}=\dfrac{-13}{\sqrt{174}}$ (B). (Strictly the acute angle between the lines would use $+13$, but that is not an option; the school's key is B.)

questions.question: Consider $z^6=1$. Which of the following are the roots of the equation?
questions.answer: The six sixth roots of unity are evenly spaced around the unit circle, $\dfrac{2\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ apart, so they are $\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{k\pi}{3}$ — this rules out the $\frac{k\pi}{6}$ options (B), (D). Option (A) gives $\operatorname{cis}(\pm\pi)=-1$ twice and omits $1$ (which is a root), so (A) fails. The answer is (C). (Written here with $\operatorname{cis}\theta=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$; the original options used $e^{i\theta}$.)

questions.question:
Consider the statement:
$$\forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ \exists y\in\mathbb{R}\ \text{such that}\ x^y>1.$$
Which of the following is the negation of the statement above?
questions.answer: Negating each part: $\forall x\to\exists x$, $\exists y\to\forall y$, and $x^y>1\to x^y\le1$. The negation is $\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R},\ x^y\le 1$ (B).

questions.question:
A particle moving along a horizontal line has acceleration
$$a=\frac{12-4x}{x^3}$$
where $x$ is the displacement of the particle. The particle starts from rest at $x=6$.

Which of the following describes the velocity of the particle?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=\dfrac{12}{x^3}-\dfrac{4}{x^2}$, so $\tfrac12v^2=-\dfrac{6}{x^2}+\dfrac4x+C$, i.e. $v^2=-\dfrac{12}{x^2}+\dfrac8x+2C$. At $x=6$, $v=0$: $0=-\dfrac{12}{36}+\dfrac86+2C=1+2C$, so $2C=-1$. Hence $v^2=-\dfrac{12}{x^2}+\dfrac8x-1$ (D). (The school's working has a slip, writing $C=0$ before correctly arriving at the constant $-1$.)

questions.question:
Let $\omega$ be a non-real cube root of unity.

Which of the following is equivalent to $\left(1+2\omega-\omega^2+\omega^3\right)^5$?
questions.answer: Since $\omega^3=1$ and $\omega$ is non-real, $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$. Then $1+2\omega-\omega^2+\omega^3=2+2\omega-\omega^2=2(1+\omega)-\omega^2=-2\omega^2-\omega^2=-3\omega^2$. So $(-3\omega^2)^5=-243\omega^{10}=-243\omega\,(\omega^3)^3=-243\omega$ (A).

questions.question:
Let $z$ be a complex number such that $\operatorname{Im}(z)\ne0$.

Which of the following expressions is equivalent to $\dfrac{8z\overline{z}}{(\overline{z}-z)^2}$?
questions.answer:
$z\overline z=|z|^2=[\operatorname{Re}z]^2+[\operatorname{Im}z]^2$ and $\overline z-z=-2i\operatorname{Im}(z)$, so $(\overline z-z)^2=-4[\operatorname{Im}z]^2$. Then
$$\frac{8z\overline z}{(\overline z-z)^2}=\frac{8\left([\operatorname{Re}z]^2+[\operatorname{Im}z]^2\right)}{-4[\operatorname{Im}z]^2}=-2\left(\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2+1\right)=-2-2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2\ \text{(C)}.$$

questions.question: Which position vector best describes the curve in the diagram? (The solid part of the curve and the dashed part together form the curve; the arrows show it continuing.)
questions.answer: On the solid branch, as the curve climbs up the $z$-axis ($z\to+\infty$), $x\to0^+$ and $y\to0^+$. Test each option as $z\to\infty$: (A) $z=e^{-t}\to\infty$ needs $t\to-\infty$, but then $x=t\to-\infty$; (B) $z=e^t\to\infty$ needs $t\to\infty$, but then $x=t\to\infty$; (C) $z=t\to\infty$, but then $y=-\frac1t\to0^-$; (D) $z=-t\to\infty$ needs $t\to-\infty$, giving $x=e^t\to0^+$ and $y=-\frac1t\to0^+$. Only (D) fits (D).

questions.question:
Which of the following integrals is equivalent to
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{x}{1+\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\ ?$$
questions.answer:
Let $I$ be the integral. Using $\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx$ with $a=\frac\pi2$ (so $\sin(\frac\pi2-x)=\cos x$, $\cos(\frac\pi2-x)=\sin x$):
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\frac\pi2-x}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\,dx=\frac\pi2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x+\cos x}-I.$$
So $2I=\dfrac\pi2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin x+\cos x}$ and $I=\dfrac\pi4\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin x+\cos x}$ (D).

questions.question:
Consider the statement:

*Period 0 is cancelled if and only if there is an excursion.*

Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The negation is ‘Period 0 being cancelled does not imply that there is an excursion’.
A counterexample is ‘There is no excursion and Period 0 is cancelled’.
A counterexample is ‘Period 0 is not cancelled and there is an excursion’.
questions.answer:
Let $p$: ‘Period 0 is cancelled’ and $q$: ‘there is an excursion’. The statement is $(p\Rightarrow q)\wedge(q\Rightarrow p)$, whose negation is $(p\wedge
eg q)\vee(q\wedge
eg p)$ — an ‘or’ statement, so (A) is true. (C) is the case $p\wedge
eg q$ and (D) is the case $q\wedge
eg p$, so both are genuine counterexamples. (B) gives only one of the two parts of the negation (it negates just $p\Rightarrow q$), so it is not the negation: (B) is FALSE.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{-3+i}{1-2i}$, showing all working out.
Given that $w=2-i\left(2\sqrt3\right)$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=\dfrac\pi3$, find the exact value of $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$.
questions.answer:
$w=2-2\sqrt3\,i$ is in the fourth quadrant with $\tan\theta=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3}{2}=-\sqrt3$, so $\operatorname{Arg}(w)=-\dfrac\pi3$.

Using $\arg(zw)=\arg z+\arg w$:
$$\operatorname{Arg}(z)=\frac\pi3-\left(-\frac\pi3\right)=\frac{2\pi}{3},$$
which lies in $(-\pi,\pi]$. Check: $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=\frac{2\pi}3-\frac\pi3=\frac\pi3$ ✓.

*Note: the school's solution gives $-\frac\pi3$, which is wrong (it takes $\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, ignoring that $w$ is in the fourth quadrant); $-\frac\pi3$ would give $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=-\frac{2\pi}3$.*

questions.question: The complex numbers $z_1=2-3i$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ are roots of the polynomial $p(z)=z^3-8z^2+29z-52$. Find $z_2$ and $z_3$.
questions.answer:
$p(z)$ has real coefficients, so the conjugate $2+3i$ is also a root. Take $z_2=2+3i$. By the sum of roots,
$$(2-3i)+(2+3i)+z_3=-(-8)=8\ \Rightarrow\ z_3=4.$$
Check by product of roots: $(2-3i)(2+3i)(4)=13\times4=52$ ✓.

So $z_2=2+3i$ and $z_3=4$ (in either order). (The school's final line mistakenly lists $2-3i$ again, but its working finds $2+3i$ and $4$.)

questions.question: Find the square roots of $21-20i$.
questions.answer:
Let $(x+iy)^2=21-20i$ with $x,y$ real. Then $x^2-y^2=21$ and $2xy=-20$, so $xy=-10$.

By inspection $x=5,\ y=-2$ works ($25-4=21$, $5\times(-2)=-10$), and so does $x=-5,\ y=2$. (Algebraically: $x^2-\frac{100}{x^2}=21\Rightarrow x^4-21x^2-100=0\Rightarrow(x^2-25)(x^2+4)=0\Rightarrow x=\pm5$.)

The square roots are $5-2i$ and $-5+2i$.

questions.question: Prove that $\dfrac32k^2-6k-\dfrac{63}2$ is divisible by $12$ for all positive odd integers $k$.
questions.answer:
Let $k=2a+1$ where $a\ge0$ is an integer. Then
$$\frac32(2a+1)^2-6(2a+1)-\frac{63}2=\frac32\left(4a^2+4a+1\right)-12a-6-\frac{63}2=6a^2-6a-36=6\left(a^2-a-6\right)=6\left(a(a-1)-6\right).$$
Now $a(a-1)$ is a product of two consecutive integers, so it is even: $a(a-1)=2m$ for some integer $m$. Hence the expression equals $6(2m-6)=12(m-3)$, where $m-3$ is an integer, so it is divisible by $12$. $\blacksquare$

*(The school's justification, “one of the consecutive integers must be negative”, is not the right reason; evenness of $a(a-1)$ is what is needed.)*

questions.question:
By decomposing $\dfrac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}$ into partial fractions, show that
$$\frac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}=\frac{3x+6}{x^2+2}-\frac{3}{x+1}.$$
questions.answer:
Let $\dfrac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}=\dfrac{Ax+B}{x^2+2}+\dfrac{C}{x+1}$. Then $9x=(Ax+B)(x+1)+C(x^2+2)$.

- $x=-1$: $-9=3C\Rightarrow C=-3$.
- $x=0$: $0=B+2C\Rightarrow B=6$.
- $x=1$: $9=2(A+B)+3C=2(A+6)-9\Rightarrow A=3$.

Therefore $\dfrac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}=\dfrac{3x+6}{x^2+2}-\dfrac3{x+1}$.

questions.question: Using the result $\dfrac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}=\dfrac{3x+6}{x^2+2}-\dfrac{3}{x+1}$, find $\displaystyle\int\frac{9x}{(x^2+2)(x+1)}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$$\int\left(\frac{3x}{x^2+2}+\frac{6}{x^2+2}-\frac3{x+1}\right)dx=\frac32\ln(x^2+2)+\frac{6}{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{\sqrt2}-3\ln|x+1|+C,$$
that is $\dfrac32\ln(x^2+2)+3\sqrt2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt2}-3\ln|x+1|+C$.

questions.question: Using an appropriate substitution, find $\displaystyle\int\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{2x}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $u=1+\sqrt{2x}$. Then $\dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2x}}$, so $dx=\sqrt{2x}\,du=(u-1)\,du$.
$$\int\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{2x}}\,dx=\int\frac{2(u-1)}{u}\,du=2\int\left(1-\frac1u\right)du=2u-2\ln|u|+C=2\sqrt{2x}-2\ln\left(1+\sqrt{2x}\right)+C$$
(the constant $2$ from $2u$ is absorbed into $C$).

questions.question:
Consider the statement: *For all irrational numbers $p$, the number $\left(\dfrac13-5p\right)$ is irrational.*

State the negation of this statement.
questions.answer: There exists an irrational number $p$ such that $\dfrac13-5p$ is rational.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that: for all irrational numbers $p$, the number $\left(\dfrac13-5p\right)$ is irrational.
questions.answer:
Assume the negation: there is an irrational $p$ with $\dfrac13-5p$ rational. Then $\dfrac13-5p=\dfrac ab$ for some integers $a,b$ with $b\ne0$. Solving for $p$:
$$5p=\frac13-\frac ab=\frac{b-3a}{3b}\ \Rightarrow\ p=\frac{b-3a}{15b}.$$
Since $b-3a$ and $15b$ are integers with $15b\neq0$, $p$ is rational. This contradicts $p$ being irrational. Hence the assumption is false and the statement is true. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Rosa’s office chair oscillates along a straight path with an amplitude of $3$ cm. The acceleration $\ddot x$ cm/s$^2$ of the chair is $\ddot x=20-4x$, where $x$ is the displacement of the chair from her desk.

Briefly explain why the chair is undergoing simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: $\ddot x=20-4x=-2^2(x-5)$, which has the form $\ddot x=-n^2(x-c)$ with $n=2$ and centre of motion $c=5$. Acceleration is proportional to, and opposite in direction to, the displacement from the centre $x=5$, so the motion is simple harmonic.

questions.question:
The acceleration of Rosa’s office chair is $\ddot x=20-4x$ (cm/s$^2$), where $x$ cm is its displacement from her desk, and the amplitude of the oscillation is $3$ cm. By integrating $\ddot x$ with respect to $x$, show that the velocity of the chair is given by
$$v^2=-4\left((x-5)^2-9\right).$$
questions.answer:
The centre of motion is $x=5$ and the amplitude is $3$, so the chair is momentarily at rest ($v=0$) at $x=5\pm3$, e.g. $x=2$.

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=20-4x\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac12v^2=20x-2x^2+C.$$
At $x=2$, $v=0$: $0=40-8+C\Rightarrow C=-32$. So $\tfrac12v^2=20x-2x^2-32$ and
$$v^2=40x-4x^2-64=-4\left(x^2-10x+16\right)=-4\left((x-5)^2-9\right).\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question: The velocity of Rosa’s office chair (displacement $x$ cm from her desk) satisfies $v^2=-4\left((x-5)^2-9\right)$. Find the fastest speed that the chair reaches.
questions.answer: The speed is greatest at the centre of motion $x=5$, where $v^2=-4(0-9)=36$, so $|v|=6$. The fastest speed is $6$ cm/s.

questions.question: Rosa’s office chair oscillates in simple harmonic motion with $\ddot x=20-4x$ (cm/s$^2$) and amplitude $3$ cm, where $x$ cm is the displacement from her desk. Given that the chair starts at the position closest to the desk, determine a possible equation for the displacement of the chair.
questions.answer:
The centre is $c=5$, $n=2$ and the amplitude is $3$, so the chair moves between $x=2$ and $x=8$. It starts at the closest position $x=2$ at $t=0$, so
$$x=5-3\cos 2t.$$

questions.question: Rosa’s office chair has displacement $x=5-3\cos2t$ cm from her desk at time $t$ seconds. Determine whether the chair is moving towards or away from the desk after $\dfrac{37\pi}{24}$ seconds. Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
$\dot x=6\sin2t$. When $t=\dfrac{37\pi}{24}$, $2t=\dfrac{37\pi}{12}$ and $\dot x=6\sin\dfrac{37\pi}{12}=-6\sin\dfrac{\pi}{12}\approx-1.55<0$. The displacement from the desk is decreasing, so the chair is moving **towards** the desk.

*Alternative:* the period is $\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi}2<\frac{37\pi}{24}<2\pi$. The chair starts at its minimum $x=2$, is at its maximum $x=8$ after $\frac{\pi}{2}$, back at $x=2$ at $\pi$, and at $x=8$ again at $\frac{3\pi}{2}$; after that it is returning towards the desk.

questions.question:
The complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$ are represented by the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=2OB$ and $\angle AOB=\dfrac\pi6$ as shown in the Argand diagram. It is given that $z_1=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$.

Express $z_2$ in polar form, in terms of $r$ and $\theta$.
questions.answer:
$|z_2|=OB=\tfrac12OA=\tfrac12r$, and $B$ is $\dfrac\pi6$ anticlockwise from $A$, so $\arg z_2=\theta+\dfrac\pi6$. Equivalently $z_2=\tfrac12\cdot z_1\cdot\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi6$ (dilation by $\frac12$, rotation by $\frac\pi6$). Therefore
$$z_2=\frac r2\left(\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi6\right)+i\sin\left(\theta+\frac\pi6\right)\right).$$
(The original question asks for exponential form $\tfrac r2e^{i(\theta+\pi/6)}$; polar form is used here.)

questions.question:
The complex numbers $z_1=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ and $z_2=\dfrac r2\left(\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac\pi6\right)+i\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac\pi6\right)\right)$ are represented by the points $A$ and $B$ respectively, where $r>0$ and $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$ (so $OA=2OB$ and $\angle AOB=\dfrac\pi6$, as in the diagram).

Let $C$ be the point such that $ABOC$ is a parallelogram and $\angle AOC=\phi$, where $0<\phi<\dfrac\pi2$. Consider the complex number $w$ for which $z_1w$ represents $C$.

By finding $w$, calculate $\phi$ correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer:
Opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal and parallel, so $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{BA}$, i.e. $z_1w=z_1-z_2$. Then
$$z_1w=z_1\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{cis}\tfrac\pi6\right)\ \Rightarrow\ w=1-\tfrac12\left(\cos\tfrac\pi6+i\sin\tfrac\pi6\right)=\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)-\frac14i.$$
Multiplying $z_1$ by $w$ rotates $OA$ through $\arg w$, so $\phi=|\operatorname{Arg}w|=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1/4}{1-\sqrt3/4}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt3}\approx0.4153$.

Hence $\phi\approx0.42$ radians.

questions.question:
Consider the region of the complex plane defined by
$$|z-2+2i|\le4\quad\text{and}\quad-\frac\pi3\le\operatorname{Arg}(z-1+3i)\le\frac\pi4.$$
On an Argand diagram, clearly sketch the region.
questions.answer: $|z-(2-2i)|\le4$ is the closed disc with centre $2-2i$ and radius $4$. $-\frac\pi3\le\operatorname{Arg}(z-(1-3i))\le\frac\pi4$ is the wedge between the rays from $1-3i$ at angles $-\frac\pi3$ and $\frac\pi4$ to the positive real direction, with the point $1-3i$ itself excluded (its argument is undefined). The point $1-3i$ lies inside the circle, so the region is the part of the disc inside the wedge, shown shaded below (open circle at $1-3i$).

questions.question:
Let $w$ represent any complex number that lies in the region defined by
$$|z-2+2i|\le4\quad\text{and}\quad-\frac\pi3\le\operatorname{Arg}(z-1+3i)\le\frac\pi4.$$
Find the possible range of values for $\operatorname{Arg}(w)$, giving your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer:
The region is the part of the disc with centre $2-2i$, radius $4$ inside the wedge from the point $1-3i$ (excluded) between the rays at $-\frac\pi3$ and $\frac\pi4$.

*Maximum:* the origin lies inside the circle, so $\operatorname{Arg}$ increases anticlockwise round the arc; the largest value occurs where the upper ray meets the circle, at $z_1$. The ray is $y=x-4$; substituting in $(x-2)^2+(y+2)^2=16$ gives $2(x-2)^2=16$, $x=2+2\sqrt2$ (the right-hand intersection), $y=-2+2\sqrt2$. So $z_1=(2+2\sqrt2)+(-2+2\sqrt2)i$ and $\operatorname{Arg}z_1=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{-2+2\sqrt2}{2+2\sqrt2}\approx0.17$.

*Minimum:* arguments decrease towards the apex $1-3i$, which is excluded, so $\operatorname{Arg}w>\operatorname{Arg}(1-3i)=-\tan^{-1}3\approx-1.25$.

Hence $-1.25<\operatorname{Arg}(w)\le0.17$.

questions.question: Prove that $|a-b|+|c-b|+|c-d|\ge a-d$.
questions.answer:
Using $|c-b|=|b-c|$ and the triangle inequality $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$ twice:
$$|a-b|+|b-c|+|c-d|\ge|(a-b)+(b-c)|+|c-d|=|a-c|+|c-d|\ge|(a-c)+(c-d)|=|a-d|.$$
Finally $|a-d|\ge a-d$ (if $a\ge d$ then $|a-d|=a-d$; if $a<d$ then $|a-d|>0>a-d$). Hence $|a-b|+|c-b|+|c-d|\ge a-d$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
By considering the contrapositive, prove that for all $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and where $n\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$\text{if } a+b\ge2n+1,\ \text{then } a\ge n+1\ \text{or}\ b\ge n+1.$$
questions.answer:
The contrapositive is: if $a<n+1$ **and** $b<n+1$, then $a+b<2n+1$ (negating “$a\ge n+1$ or $b\ge n+1$” gives “$a<n+1$ and $b<n+1$”).

Since $a,b,n$ are integers, $a<n+1$ means $a\le n$, and likewise $b\le n$. Adding, $a+b\le2n<2n+1$. So the contrapositive is true, and therefore the original implication is true. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Use mathematical induction to prove that, for all integers $n\ge3$,
$$(3n)!<(n!)^3\times27^n.$$
questions.answer:
Let $P(n)$ be the proposition $(3n)!<(n!)^3\times27^n$.

**Base case** $n=3$: LHS $=9!=362\,880$; RHS $=(3!)^3\times27^3=216\times19\,683=4\,251\,528$. LHS $<$ RHS, so $P(3)$ is true.

**Inductive step:** assume $P(k)$ for some integer $k\ge3$: $(3k)!<(k!)^3\times27^k$. Required: $(3k+3)!<((k+1)!)^3\times27^{k+1}$.
$$(3k+3)!=(3k+3)(3k+2)(3k+1)(3k)!<(3k+3)(3k+2)(3k+1)(k!)^3\,27^k.$$
Now $(3k+3)(3k+2)(3k+1)=3(k+1)(3k+2)(3k+1)$ and $(3k+2)(3k+1)=9k^2+9k+2<9k^2+18k+9=9(k+1)^2$. Hence
$$(3k+3)(3k+2)(3k+1)<27(k+1)^3,$$
so $(3k+3)!<27(k+1)^3(k!)^3\,27^k=\left((k+1)!\right)^3\,27^{k+1}$. So $P(k+1)$ is true whenever $P(k)$ is.

By mathematical induction, $P(n)$ holds for all integers $n\ge3$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Consider the rectangular prism in the diagram, with $O$ at the origin and $A$, $B$, $C$ on the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes respectively; $P$ is the vertex of the prism opposite $O$. Let $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ be the non-zero position vectors of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$.

Using vector methods, prove that triangle $ACP$ **cannot** be a right-angled triangle.
questions.answer:
Since the axes are perpendicular, $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=0$, and $P$ has position vector $\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$. Check each angle.

*At $A$:* $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf b+\mathbf c$.
$$\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c+|\mathbf c|^2-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c=|\mathbf c|^2\ne0.$$
*At $C$:* $\overrightarrow{CA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf c$, $\overrightarrow{CP}=\mathbf a+\mathbf b$.
$$\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CP}=|\mathbf a|^2+\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=|\mathbf a|^2\ne0.$$
*At $P$:* $\overrightarrow{PA}=-\mathbf b-\mathbf c$, $\overrightarrow{PC}=-\mathbf a-\mathbf b$.
$$\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{PC}=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+|\mathbf b|^2+\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c=|\mathbf b|^2\ne0.$$
No pair of sides is perpendicular (each dot product is the square of a non-zero length), so triangle $ACP$ cannot be right-angled. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{3\sqrt2}^{6}\frac{dx}{x^3\sqrt{x^2-9}}$.
questions.answer:
Let $x=3\sec\theta$, $dx=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$. When $x=3\sqrt2$, $\theta=\frac\pi4$; when $x=6$, $\theta=\frac\pi3$. Also $\sqrt{x^2-9}=3\tan\theta$.
$$\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\frac{3\sec\theta\tan\theta}{27\sec^3\theta\cdot3\tan\theta}\,d\theta=\frac1{27}\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac1{54}\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac1{54}\left[\theta+\tfrac12\sin2\theta\right]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}.$$
$$=\frac1{54}\left[\left(\frac\pi3+\frac{\sqrt3}4\right)-\left(\frac\pi4+\frac12\right)\right]=\frac1{54}\left(\frac\pi{12}+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}-\frac12\right)=\frac{\pi+3\sqrt3-6}{648}.$$

questions.question:
A rock band is performing at a small arena shaped as a hemisphere with a diameter of $26$ metres. Let the centre of the arena be the origin $O$. A mirror is placed at the point $R(a,b,c)$ on the arena’s roof (on the surface of the hemisphere). A light is shone from the point $P(-46,5,0)$ outside the arena to the mirror at $R$.

Given that $PR\perp OR$, prove that $46a-5b+169=0$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{PR}=\begin{pmatrix}a+46\\b-5\\c\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix}$. Since $PR\perp OR$,
$$\overrightarrow{PR}\cdot\overrightarrow{OR}=0:\quad a^2+46a+b^2-5b+c^2=0.\qquad(1)$$
$R$ lies on the sphere of radius $13$ centred at $O$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2=169$. $\quad(2)$

Substituting (2) into (1): $169+46a-5b=0$, i.e. $46a-5b+169=0$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: A hemispherical arena has diameter $26$ m and centre $O$ at the origin. A mirror is at $R(a,b,c)$ on its roof (on the sphere surface, $c>0$), where $46a-5b+169=0$. If the mirror at $R$ is directly above a seat in the arena located at $(k,-3,0)$, find the coordinates of $R$.
questions.answer:
$R$ is directly above $(k,-3,0)$, so $a=k$, $b=-3$. Then $46a+15+169=0\Rightarrow a=-4$. On the sphere, $a^2+b^2+c^2=169$: $16+9+c^2=169\Rightarrow c^2=144$, and $c>0$ (the roof is above the ground), so $c=12$.

$R=(-4,-3,12)$.

questions.question:
A mirror is at $R(-4,-3,12)$ on the roof of a hemispherical arena with centre at the origin $O$. The mirror is angled so that light is reflected upwards from $R$ in the direction of $\overrightarrow{OR}$. Fireworks are shot along the path
$$\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}-14\\-10\\0\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\5\end{pmatrix},\quad\mu\in\mathbb{R}.$$
Determine whether the trajectory of the fireworks will cross through the reflected ray of light.
questions.answer:
The reflected ray is on the line through $R$ with direction $\overrightarrow{OR}=(-4,-3,12)$: $\mathbf r=\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-3\\12\end{pmatrix}$ (this line passes through $O$ and $R$). Set $\mathbf f=\mathbf r$:
$$-14+2\mu=-4\lambda\ (3),\qquad-10+\mu=-3\lambda\ (4),\qquad5\mu=12\lambda\ (5).$$
$(3)-2\times(4)$: $6=2\lambda$, so $\lambda=3$; then from (4), $\mu=1$.
Check in (5): LHS $=5\mu=5$ but RHS $=12\lambda=36$, so the equations are inconsistent. The directions $(2,1,5)$ and $(-4,-3,12)$ are not parallel and there is no intersection, so the lines are skew.

The trajectory of the fireworks does **not** cross the reflected ray of light.

questions.question: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+ac+bc$.
questions.answer: Since squares are non-negative, $(a-b)^2\ge0$, giving $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$. Similarly $a^2+c^2\ge2ac$ and $b^2+c^2\ge2bc$. Adding the three: $2(a^2+b^2+c^2)\ge2(ab+ac+bc)$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+ac+bc$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers. Given that $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+ac+bc$, prove that $a^3+b^3+c^3\ge3abc$.
questions.answer:
Multiply both sides of $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+ac+bc$ by $a+b+c>0$:
$$a^3+b^3+c^3+\left(a^2b+a^2c+ab^2+b^2c+ac^2+bc^2\right)\ge\left(a^2b+a^2c+ab^2+b^2c+ac^2+bc^2\right)+3abc.$$
Cancelling the common bracket: $a^3+b^3+c^3\ge3abc$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $ac(a+c)+ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)\ge6abc$.
(You may use $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$ for real $a,b$.)
questions.answer:
Since $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$ and $c>0$: $c(a^2+b^2)\ge2abc$. Similarly $b(a^2+c^2)\ge2abc$ and $a(b^2+c^2)\ge2abc$. Adding,
$$a^2c+b^2c+a^2b+bc^2+ab^2+ac^2\ge6abc,$$
and the left side equals $ac(a+c)+ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)$. $\blacksquare$

(Equivalently the difference is $a(b-c)^2+b(a-c)^2+c(a-b)^2\ge0$. The school’s solution reaches the result by applying part (ii) to $\frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c$, multiplying inequalities and substituting cube roots; the direct proof above is simpler.)

questions.question:
Consider the series
$$C=1+\cos\theta+\cos2\theta+\cdots+\cos(n-1)\theta,\qquad S=\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\cdots+\sin(n-1)\theta.$$
Given that $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $C+iS=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$ where $z\ne1$.
questions.answer:
By de Moivre's theorem, $z^k=\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta$. So
$$C+iS=1+(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)+\cdots+(\cos(n-1)\theta+i\sin(n-1)\theta)=1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^{n-1}.$$
This is a geometric series with first term $1$ and ratio $z\neq1$, so $C+iS=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Let $C=1+\cos\theta+\cdots+\cos(n-1)\theta$, $S=\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\cdots+\sin(n-1)\theta$ and $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Using $C+iS=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$, show that
$$\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\cdots+\sin(n-1)\theta=\frac{(\sin\theta-\sin n\theta)+\sin[(n-1)\theta]}{2(1-\cos\theta)}.$$
questions.answer:
By de Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of $1-z=(1-\cos\theta)-i\sin\theta$:
$$C+iS=\frac{\left[(1-\cos n\theta)-i\sin n\theta\right]\left[(1-\cos\theta)+i\sin\theta\right]}{(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta}.$$
The denominator is $2-2\cos\theta$. The imaginary part of the numerator is
$$(1-\cos n\theta)\sin\theta-\sin n\theta(1-\cos\theta)=\sin\theta-\sin n\theta+(\sin n\theta\cos\theta-\cos n\theta\sin\theta)=\sin\theta-\sin n\theta+\sin(n-1)\theta.$$
Equating imaginary parts, $S=\dfrac{(\sin\theta-\sin n\theta)+\sin[(n-1)\theta]}{2(1-\cos\theta)}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Let $I_{3n+2}=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{3n+2}e^{x^3}\,dx$, where $n$ is an integer with $n\ge1$. Prove that $I_{3n+2}=\dfrac e3-nI_{3n-1}$.
questions.answer:
Integrate by parts with $u=x^{3n}$, $v'=x^2e^{x^3}$, so $u'=3nx^{3n-1}$, $v=\tfrac13e^{x^3}$:
$$I_{3n+2}=\left[\tfrac13x^{3n}e^{x^3}\right]_0^1-\int_0^1 n\,x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}\,dx=\tfrac13e-nI_{3n-1}.\ \blacksquare$$
(The boundary term at $x=0$ is $0$ because $n\ge1$. The paper states $n\ge0$, but for $n=0$ the formula would involve the divergent $I_{-1}$ and the lower boundary term is $\tfrac13\ne0$, so $n\ge1$ is needed.)

questions.question: Let $I_{3n+2}=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{3n+2}e^{x^3}\,dx$. Given the reduction formula $I_{3n+2}=\dfrac e3-nI_{3n-1}$ (for $n\ge1$), find $I_8$ as an exact value.
questions.answer:
Taking $n=2$: $I_8=\dfrac e3-2I_5$. Taking $n=1$: $I_5=\dfrac e3-I_2$, where
$$I_2=\int_0^1x^2e^{x^3}\,dx=\left[\tfrac13e^{x^3}\right]_0^1=\frac{e-1}3.$$
So $I_5=\dfrac e3-\dfrac{e-1}3=\dfrac13$ and $I_8=\dfrac e3-\dfrac23=\dfrac{e-2}{3}$.

questions.question:
Let $I_{3n+2}=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{3n+2}e^{x^3}\,dx$ for integers $n\ge1$, and recall $I_{3n+2}=\dfrac e3-nI_{3n-1}$. Using this, prove that
$$3\int_0^1(1+x^3)\,x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}\,dx\le e.$$
questions.answer:
Expand: $3\displaystyle\int_0^1(1+x^3)x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}dx=3\left(\int_0^1x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}dx+\int_0^1x^{3n+2}e^{x^3}dx\right)=3\left(I_{3n-1}+I_{3n+2}\right)$.

Using the reduction formula: $3\left(I_{3n-1}+\dfrac e3-nI_{3n-1}\right)=e-3(n-1)I_{3n-1}$.

For $0\le x\le1$ and $n\ge1$, $x^{3n-1}\ge0$ and $e^{x^3}>0$, so $I_{3n-1}=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}dx\ge0$. Also $n-1\ge0$, so $3(n-1)I_{3n-1}\ge0$. Therefore
$$3\int_0^1(1+x^3)x^{3n-1}e^{x^3}\,dx=e-3(n-1)I_{3n-1}\le e.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
By considering a possible graph of $y=f(x)$, prove that:

If $f$ is a continuous function where $f'(x)>0$, $f''(x)<0$ and $f(0)=0$, then
$$\int_0^af(x)\,dx+\int_0^bf^{-1}(y)\,dy\ge ab,$$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse function of $f$, $a\ge0$ and $b\ge0$.
questions.answer:
$f$ is increasing, concave down, passes through the origin, so it has an inverse. $\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx$ is the area between the curve and the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le a$, and $\displaystyle\int_0^bf^{-1}(y)\,dy$ is the area between the curve and the $y$-axis for $0\le y\le b$ (since $y=f(x)\Leftrightarrow x=f^{-1}(y)$). The rectangle $[0,a]\times[0,b]$ has area $ab$.

**Case 1: $f(a)=b$.** The two areas fit together exactly to fill the rectangle: the sum equals $ab$.

**Case 2: $f(a)<b$.** The area to the left of the curve for $0\le y\le b$ extends beyond $x=a$ by an extra region $A_1>0$ (above the curve, to the right of $x=a$), so the sum is $ab+A_1>ab$.

**Case 3: $f(a)>b$.** The area under the curve for $0\le x\le a$ extends above the line $y=b$ by an extra region $A_2>0$, so the sum is $ab+A_2>ab$.

**Trivial case:** if $a=0$ or $b=0$, then $ab=0$ and both integrals are $\ge0$ (as $f,f^{-1}\ge0$ on $[0,\infty)$), so the sum is $\ge ab$.

In every case $\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx+\int_0^bf^{-1}(y)\,dy\ge ab$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Given the result: if $f$ is continuous with $f'(x)>0$, $f''(x)<0$ and $f(0)=0$, then
$$\int_0^af(x)\,dx+\int_0^bf^{-1}(y)\,dy\ge ab\quad(a,b\ge0),$$
prove that
$$\tan^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)\ge\frac\pi6+\ln\left(\frac{15}{16}\right).$$
questions.answer:
Take $f(x)=\tan^{-1}x$ for $x\ge0$: $f(0)=0$, $f'(x)=\dfrac1{1+x^2}>0$ and $f''(x)=\dfrac{-2x}{(1+x^2)^2}<0$ for $x>0$, so the result applies. $f^{-1}(y)=\tan y$.

Integrate by parts: $\displaystyle\int_0^a\tan^{-1}x\,dx=\left[x\tan^{-1}x\right]_0^a-\int_0^a\frac{x}{1+x^2}dx=a\tan^{-1}a-\tfrac12\ln(1+a^2)$, and $\displaystyle\int_0^b\tan y\,dy=\left[-\ln\cos y\right]_0^b=-\ln\cos b$ (for $0\le b<\frac\pi2$).

So $a\tan^{-1}a-\tfrac12\ln(1+a^2)-\ln\cos b\ge ab$. Let $a=\tfrac12$ and $b=\tfrac\pi6$: $\cos b=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $1+a^2=\tfrac54$:
$$\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac12-\tfrac12\ln\tfrac54-\ln\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\ge\tfrac\pi{12}.$$
Multiply by $2$: $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12\ge\tfrac\pi6+\ln\tfrac54+2\ln\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=\tfrac\pi6+\ln\tfrac54+\ln\tfrac34=\tfrac\pi6+\ln\tfrac{15}{16}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
An object of mass $2$ kg is at a height of $90$ metres above the ground. It is dropped from rest and falls vertically downwards through a gaseous medium which exerts a resistance to the motion equal to $\dfrac{v^2}{45}$ newtons, where $v$ m s$^{-1}$ is the velocity of the object. After falling $25$ metres, the object exits the gaseous medium and continues to fall vertically downwards, subject to air resistance equal to $\dfrac v{10}$ newtons. The acceleration due to gravity is $10$ m s$^{-2}$.

Show that the object exits the gaseous medium approximately $2.34$ seconds after it was dropped.
questions.answer:
Take downwards as positive. In the gaseous medium: $2\ddot x=20-\dfrac{v^2}{45}$, so $\ddot x=\dfrac{900-v^2}{90}$.

*Speed on exit* ($v=V$ at $x=25$): $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{900-v^2}{90}$, so
$$\int_0^V\frac{v}{900-v^2}\,dv=\int_0^{25}\frac1{90}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ -\tfrac12\ln\frac{900-V^2}{900}=\frac{25}{90}\ \Rightarrow\ 900-V^2=900e^{-5/9},$$
$V^2=900\left(1-e^{-5/9}\right)$, $V\approx19.586$ m s$^{-1}$.

*Time:* $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{(30+v)(30-v)}{90}$, so (with $0\le v<30$)
$$\int_0^V\frac{1}{(30+v)(30-v)}dv=\int_0^t\frac1{90}dt\ \Rightarrow\ \frac1{60}\int_0^V\left(\frac1{30+v}+\frac1{30-v}\right)dv=\frac t{90}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac1{60}\ln\frac{30+V}{30-V}=\frac t{90}.$$
So $t=\dfrac32\ln\dfrac{30+V}{30-V}=\dfrac32\ln\dfrac{49.586}{10.414}\approx2.34$ s.

The object exits the gaseous medium about $2.34$ seconds after being dropped. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
An object $A$ of mass $2$ kg is dropped from rest at a height of $90$ m above the ground. It falls through a gaseous medium (resistance $\frac{v^2}{45}$ newtons) for its first $25$ m, i.e. between $90$ m and $65$ m above the ground, exiting it about $2.34$ s after release; below that it falls through air with resistance $\frac{v}{10}$ newtons. Take $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$.

At the same instant that $A$ is dropped, an identical second object $B$ (mass $2$ kg) is launched vertically upwards from the ground directly below, at a speed of $40$ m s$^{-1}$, subject to air resistance $\frac v{10}$ newtons, and it collides with $A$.

Determine in which medium (the gaseous medium or the air) the two objects collide. Justify your answer with the appropriate calculations.
questions.answer:
Take upwards as positive for $B$ (in air): $2\ddot x=-20-\dfrac v{10}$, so $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac{200+v}{20}$.
$$\int_{40}^{v}\frac{dv}{200+v}=-\frac1{20}\int_0^tdt\ \Rightarrow\ \ln\frac{200+v}{240}=-\frac t{20}\ \Rightarrow\ v=240e^{-t/20}-200.$$
Integrating with $x(0)=0$: $x=4800\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)-200t$.

At $t=2.34$ s (when $A$ leaves the gaseous medium): $x_B\approx62.0$ m and $v_B\approx13.5>0$, so $B$ is $62$ m above the ground and still rising.

The gaseous medium occupies heights $65$–$90$ m. At $t\approx2.34$ s, $A$ is at $65$ m and $B$ is only at $62$ m, so $B$ has not yet reached the gas (and before this time $B$ was lower still, while $A$ was in the gas above $65$ m). Hence they cannot meet in the gaseous medium. After $t\approx2.34$ s, $A$ is below $65$ m and falling while $B$ (below $A$) is rising, so they meet below $65$ m, in the air.

The two objects collide in the **air**.
